links.reason: Kalittokai 119 ends 'வால் இழை மகளிர் உயிர் பொதி அவிழ்க்கும் காலை ஆவது அறியார், மாலை என்மனார் மயங்கியோரே', the same denial as the Kural's 'மாலையோ அல்லை மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும் வேலை'. The claim is the same, and the pairing shows a single couplet holding what the kali builds through a catalogue of homing. The 'summary of an established rebuttal' rests on a dating the texts do not fix, but the compression point stands.

Purananuru 19.8-9 'குன்றத்து இறுத்த குரீஇஇனம் போல, அம்புசென்று இறுத்த அறும்புண் யானை' and Kalavazhi 8.2-3 'கடுங்கணை மெய்ம்மாய்ப்ப ... எண்ணருங் குன்றிற் குரீஇயினம் போன்றவே' share a distinctive simile: arrows in an elephant as sparrows on a hill. The frames do differ: Purananuru 19 moves on to the old women's weeping and Death fleeing (15-16), while Kalavazhi stays with the field of the 'நீர்நாடன்'.

The gift pair is real: Purananuru 361.11-12 'புரி மாலையர் பாடினிக்குப் பொலந் தாமரைப் பூம் பாணரொடு' against the idyll's lotus round which no bee hums (481) and 'பொன்னின் தொடையமை மாலை விறலியர் மலைய' (485-486). But the motive the teaches sentence ties them to, knowledge that the world does not last, appears only in Purananuru 361.20-21. The printed span has no such reason, and the cited line 466 lies outside it. 'அன்றே விடுக்கும்' (493) is haste in giving, not a response to impermanence.

Kuruntokai 305.1 'கண்தர வந்த காம ஒள்ளெரி' matches the Kural's 'தாம்காட்ட யாம்கண்டது': both say the eyes brought the sickness. The poem then carries the Kural's 'தண்டாநோய்' to 'விளிவாங்கு விளியின் அல்லது களைவோர் இலை', the cocks' fight that only death ends. The Kural's own turn, the eyes weeping for what they caused, is absent from the poem, but the extension of 'unending' holds.

In both poems the other woman names the wife only as 'புதல்வன் தாய்'. In Ainkurunuru 90 he has the bee's 'மாண்குணம்', and in Kuruntokai 8 he moves at home 'ஆடிப் பாவை போல' to his wife's wishes. Neither limits or adds a condition to the other, so qualifies does not fit. Joined, they are two jibes from the same speaker in the same situation, and their convergence is the only lesson.

The verbal link is real: Kalittokai 133.13 ''முறை' எனப்படுவது கண்ணோடாது உயிர் வௌவல்' and the Kural's 'ஓர்ந்துகண் ணோடாது ... முறை' define the same word with the same term. The teaches sentence, however, has the Kural 'tempering a stock definition' it inherited from the kali. That needs a priority neither text shows, and the kali's line sits among nine aphorisms the friend coins, not quotes.

The 'adds that he profits' claim rests entirely on one sense of 'வாரிக்குப் புக்குநின்றாய்' (34.4), and the marker flags that word as insecure. The speaker of 34 is also uncertain. Beyond that, Natrinai 200's 'பொய் பொதி கொடுஞ் சொல் ஓம்புமின்' and the venba share only the common marutham scolding of the bard, which is a shared topic rather than a development.

The image is distinctive and shared: 'இருஞ்சிறை வண்டினம் பாலை முரல' (16.2) against 'வல்லோன் தைவரும் வள்ளுயிர்ப் பாலை நரம்புஆர்த் தன்ன வண்டினம் முரலும்' (355.4-5). In the venba the bees cheer the man's 'விரும்புநாம் செல்லும் இடம்'. In the Akananuru they mark the season in which she rehearses her reproach for his going ('அருள்இலை யாகி'). So the same sound does serve opposite moods.

Kuruntokai 73 has the Kosar cut Nannan's 'நறுமா' and drive him out ('நாட்டிற் போக்கிய'). The preface has the Cheral behead 'பெருவாயில் நன்னனை' and fell his 'பொன்படு வாகை'. These are two different deeds, not incompatible claims: nothing in either says the tree was his only guardian tree, or that the Kosar killed him. The shared motif, an enemy felling Nannan's tree, is real, but the tension, and the teaches sentence built on it, are manufactured.

Ainkurunuru 80 puts the first-rain bath with women ('நலத்தகு மகளிர்க்குத் தோள்துணை யாகித் தலைப்பெயல் செம்புனல் ஆடி') behind his red eyes. Kalittokai 98 gives the husband the bath as his alibi ('வையை வரு புனல் ஆடத் தவிர்ந்தேன்', 10-11), and the wife turns the flood part by part into the woman (14-19). The pair does show the flood-bath working as excuse in one poem and as evidence in the other.

The idyll gives the patron's gift an explicit reason: 'நில்லா வுலகத்து நிலைமை தூக்கி யந்நிலை யணுகல் வேண்டி' (466-467). It is given at once, 'நின்னிலை தெரியா வளவை' (464). This is the Kural's 'அற்கா இயல்பிற்றுச் செல்வம் ... அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்' enacted as a king's habit. The idyll weighs the world rather than wealth, and 'before it became a rule' assumes a priority, but the pairing of motive and immediacy is specific.

links.reason: Both friends set the same road-sign on the man's path: an elephant breaking a yaa to feed others. In Akananuru 59 it is 'மடப்பிடி உணீஇயர் ... யாஅம் ஒற்றி', set against 'உள்ளார்'. In Kuruntokai 255 it is 'பெருநிரை உறுபசி தீர்க்கும்', set beside 'தங்கடன் இறீஇயர் எண்ணி'. The contrast of mate and herd is real and teaches something. But neither poem limits the other, so the type is a shared image turned two ways, not qualifies.

In Kuruntokai 229 the onlookers praise destiny once the match is made ('நல்லைமன் றம்ம பாலே'). In 366 the friend uses destiny beforehand as an argument: 'பால்வரைந் தமைத்த லல்ல தவர்வயிற் சால்பளந் தறிதற் கியாஅம் யாரோ'. The contrast between explaining after the event and persuading before it holds. It extends the idea of பால் rather than putting a condition on it, and lines 5-6 of 366 are obscure.
links.text_issue: 366.5-6 'உள்ளகை பழுத கண்ணள்' is hard to construe; line 3 repaired from another edition

links.reason: In the Kural the town calls him 'ஏதிலர்' and 'இகந்துறைவர்': it blames him, which takes her side, and she defends him. So the Kural's town is not hostile gossip about her either, and 'blame against pity' misstates the contrast. Kuruntokai 289.7-8 'அவர்திறத் திரங்கு நம்மினும் நந்திறத் திரங்குமிவ் வழங்கல் ஊரே' shows the pitying town by itself. The pairing adds little, and line 6 is obscure.
links.text_issue: 289.6 'பட்ட மாரி படாஅக் கண்ணும்' is hard to construe

links.reason: The shared pair of terms is real: 'கிழமை ... பழமை' in 134.1-2 against the Kural's 'பழைமை ... கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு'. The venba's question 'கேடின்மை கொல்லோ ... பயன்நோக்கிக் கொல்லோ' does set them against each other. But the teaches sentence reads the husband's many women as the 'liberties' of intimacy and adds a power asymmetry the obscure lines 3-4 do not state. That builds a thesis on a flagged-uncertain verse.
links.text_issue: 134.3-4 'கிழமை குடிநாய்கர் ... கேளா அடியேன் பெற்றா அருள்' is obscure and may be corrupt

links.reason: Purananuru 56.3-4 gives 'அடல் வெந் நாஞ்சில், பனைக்கொடி' to the conch-white god as one of four distinct gods. Paripadal 4.38-41 says to the dark god 'நின் ஒன்று உயர் கொடி பனை; நின் ஒன்று உயர் கொடி நாஞ்சில் ... நின் ஒன்றா உயர் கொடி ஒன்று இன்று'. On the reading that the hymn's 'நின்' is Mal alone, the two assign the palm banner incompatibly, and the note names that reading. The teaches sentence's point, a fixed set of four absorbed by a claim of sole lordship, is specific.

links.reason: Manimekalai 27.264-266 'தாதகிப் பூவும் கட்டியும் இட்டு மற்றும் கூட்ட மதுக் களி பிறந்தாங்கு உற்றிடும் பூதத்து உணர்வு தோன்றிடும்' and Neelakesi 858.1-2 'ஐந்துங் கூடி ... மதுமயக் காற்றலின்' both give the materialist the same simile: awareness from combined elements as intoxication from mixed ingredients. Both texts also have the awareness dissolve when the elements part (268; 858.4). That a Buddhist and a Jain refutation frame the opponent identically is a real lesson.

The Kural's point is that only seeing him with full eyes ('கண்ணாரக் கண்டபின்'), not news of him, will lift the pallor. Ainkurunuru 498 simply reports the recovery ('தோள்கவின் எய்தின தொடிநிலை நின்றன ... வந்த மாறே') once he has come. That return cures the marks of absence is the shared topic of every return poem, and the teaches sentence restates it as 'confirmation' without using the Kural's seeing-against-hearing turn.

Both close on the throbbing eye with the word இடம: 'இன்றே இறந்துகண் ஆடும் இடம்' (80.3-4) and 'நல்எழில் உண் கண்ணும் ஆடுமால், இடனே' (11.22). The contrast holds: Kalittokai reaches the omen after three pairs of tender creatures and the lizard's chirp, while the venba leans mostly on it. But the left-eye omen is a common convention, the venba also gives the road and the wealth, and the relation is a shared sign rather than one poem developing the other.

Ainthinai Aimpathu 14.3-4 has the friend say 'மாவினவு வார்போல வந்தவர் ... தாம்வினவ லுற்றதொன் றுண்டு': he came as if asking after a beast, with another question behind it. Thinaimalai 9.1 has the man call his own question deceit: 'வஞ்சமே என்னும் வகைத்தால் ஓர் மாவினாய்'. The pretext is named from both sides, by the girl's friend and by the hero, so the pair shows the beast question as an understood convention. Neither verse shows that alone.

The only link is the shared phrase 'வில்லுழுது வாழ்நர்' (17.2) against the Kural's 'வில்லேர் உழவர்'. The Kural's 'சொல்லேர் உழவர்' are counsellors whose enmity a ruler must avoid. The venba says nothing of words: its wound is 'நல்கா துறந்த', leaving without grace. Turning that into 'his word' to make the venba rank bowmen below word-men stretches it to fit the couplet.

Kar Narpathu 12 has the friend call the cloud proof ('ஐயந்தீர் காட்சி யவர்வருதல் திண்ணிதாம் ... இருங்கொண்மூ வைகலு மேரும் வலம்'). In Kuruntokai 314 the cloud comes and 'வாரார்'. These are two moments of one mullai convention, and different situations are not incompatible claims. The failed sign limits the confident one rather than contradicting it, and the lesson is close to the common topic of season and absent man.

Purananuru 38.12-17 ranks the king's land above heaven because there 'உடையோர் ஈதலும், இல்லோர் இரத்தலும் கடவ தன்மையின், கையறவு உடைத்து'. The fragment ranks Koodal above 'புத்தேள் உலகு' because it 'ஈவாரைக் கொண்டாடி, ஏற்பாரைப் பார்த்து உவக்கும்'. The argument is the same and specific (giving and receiving as what earth has that heaven lacks), here applied to a city, and the Purananuru does make the reason explicit that the fragment leaves implicit.

links.reason: The agreement is real but common: the Kural's 'உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு' and the third of Thirikadugam's three, 'ஊழினால் ஒட்டி வினைநலம் பார்ப்பானும்', are both the self-interested friend. Its key terms (பொறியறை, தட்டை, ஊழினால் ஒட்டி) are of unsure sense. The teaches sentence says the liar shows himself at the turn of fortune, but only item 2 ('கைதிரிந்து தாழ்விடத்து') is tied to the turn; item 1, the liar, is not.

Natrinai 126.8-10 'இளமையின் சிறந்த வளமையும் இல்லை; இளமை கழிந்த பின்றை வளமை காமம் தருதலும் இன்றே' makes youth's passing a reason to stay and love now. Naladiyar 16 makes the same passing a reason to refuse youth's joy: 'மன்னா மகிழ்ச்சி அறிவுடை யாளர்கண் இல்', with the lamb nibbling its slaughter garland. The premise is one and the duties drawn from it are incompatible, which is a real tension.

Both have the returning man aim at evening: the Kural's 'மனைகலந்து மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து' and Kuruntokai 250.3-4 'மாலை வாரா வளவைக் ... கடுமாக் கடவுமதி பாக'. The poem does add urgency, through her distress ('தெருமரல் உயவே') and the stag with its mate. But the Kural's distinctive turn, the king's war set against home, is not in the poem, and the speaker of the Kural is disputed. The link rests on a shared mullai motif.

Purananuru 158.5-7 lists 'கொல்லி ஆண்ட வல்வில் ஓரியும் ... காரி ஊர்ந்து ... மலையனும்' side by side among the seven givers. Natrinai 320.4-7 measures a town's uproar by 'பழ விறல் ஓரிக் கொன்ற ஒரு பெருந் தெருவில் காரி புக்க நேரார் புலம்', which makes the killing of Ori and Kaari's entry a byword. The named puram event is used for a specific akam purpose, as the note says. Whether காரி is the rider or the horse, it points to Malaiyan's side.

Both set the slipping bangle against the lord of the shore: the Kural's 'துறைவன் துறந்தமை தூற்றாகொல் ... இறைஇறவா நின்ற வளை' and Kalittokai 127.19 'இறை வளை நெகிழ்ந்த எவ்வ நோய்', with 'செறி வளை தோள் ஊர' (13). The shift of speaker and addressee is accurate. But the slipping bangle is the most common sign of separation in akam, so the pair says little beyond the shared topic.

The offered garland is shared: 'கோதை புனைகோ நினக்கு?' (111.13) against the wreath hung down her braid 'கொன்னே சூட்டி' (180.7). But line 14 'நீ ஏதிலார் தந்த பூக் கொள்வாய்' mocks him, parallel to 'பிறர் செய்த இல் இருப்பாய்' (10). It does not state a rule about girls. And her request to have her parents told (22-24) follows from her love ('யான் உற்ற நோயும் களைகுவை'), not from any such rule, so the teaches sentence's causal claims do not hold.

The Kural accuses the heart of following him because 'கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார்இல்'. Natrinai 56 gives that as the second of two guesses, the heart seeing 'தொல் நலன் இழந்த என் பொன் நிறம்' and leaving her as 'ஏதிலாட்டி' (8-10). Its first guess is the kinder one, that the heart waits 'ஒருங்கு வரல் நசையொடு' (6). The poem genuinely puts the Kural's bitter answer inside a doubt.

links.reason: Both list the same signs: the Kural's 'பைந்தொடி சோரும் ... தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்' and Kuruntokai 239.1 'தொடிநெகிழ்ந் தனவே தோள்சா யினவே'. The poem then draws a consequence the Kural does not: 'விடுநாண் உண்டோ தோழி', there is no modesty left to give up. Taking the signs as a licence to disclose is a specific development.

The shared ground is the Vaiyai bath and Koodal's gossip ('ஊர்த்து அலர்' against 'அலர்ஆ கின்று, அது பலர்வாய்ப் பட்டே'). But the fragment's lines 51-56 are knotted, and who wears the garland and who sulks is not secure. In Akananuru 296 the gossip comes from his bathing with her and his undried chest ('புலரா மார்பினை'), not from a token she displayed. Calling the fragment's woman 'the other woman' who 'wanted to be seen' builds on an insecure reading.
links.text_issue: thirattu 2.51-56 is knotted and line 49 was repaired from an encoding leftover

links.reason: The son does appear on both sides: the friend's 'காதல்அம் புதல்வன் அழும்இனி முலைக்கே' (424.4) and the husband's 'பொலந்தொடிப் புதல்வனும் பொய்தல் கற்றனன் ... யாதனின் பிரிகோ' (166.7-9). But Natrinai 166's 'why should I part?' answers a fear, and its own colophon gives the wife's distress at signs of his going, so 'unprompted' is not accurate. The son as a tie to home is otherwise a shared topic.

The verbal parallel is close: Purananuru 182.2-3 'அமிழ்தம் இயைவ தாயினும், இனிதுஎனத் தமியர் உண்டலும் இலரே ... பிறர்க்கென முயலுநர்' against Patitruppattu 38.13-16 'இனியவை பெறினே தனிதனி நுகர்கேம் தருகென விழையா ... பிறர்க்(கு)என வாழ்தி'. Applying the general class to one named king is a real lesson. But it applies the idea rather than limiting it, so qualifies is the wrong type.

Kalittokai 8.21-23 'மன்னவன் புறந்தர, வரு விருந்து ஓம்பித், தன் நகர் விழையக் கூடின் ... அது மனும் பொருளே' echoes the Kural's 'இல்வாழ்வ தெல்லாம் விருந்தோம்பி வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு'. It uses that purpose of the household as the friend's argument against the wealth journey, after three similes of unstable wealth (11, 14, 17). That is a specific application neither verse shows alone.

Both are the friend forbidding the night road for its elephants: 'இரவின் வரல்வேண்டா யானை யுடைய கரம்' against 'கான மானதர் யானையும் வழங்கும் ... இரவழங்கு சிறுநெறி'. That the ban presses for marriage is stated by Akananuru 318 alone ('மன்றல் வேண்டினும் பெறுகுவை'). The four-line verse adds nothing to it, so the pair amounts to the shared convention, and the venba's last word கரம் is itself unsure.

Purananuru 22 does make the king's wakefulness the guard of others' sleep: 'வாள் மருங்கு இலோர் காப்பு உறங்க' (13) and 'நீ துஞ்சாய் மாறே' (38). But the idyll span shows the guarded chamber at midnight ('நடுநாள்', 50; 'பள்ளி', 64), with hour-keepers hailing the king. It does not say he sleeps, so 'his own sleep needs guarding' is supplied. The sharper contrast, Purananuru 22's camp 'வாய் காவாது', is not the one drawn.

The Kural's fort is defined as 'கொண்டகூழ்த் தாகி', provisioned, and that is exactly what Purananuru 44's fort is not: 'நெல்லுடைக் கவளமொடு நெய்ம்மிதி பெறாஅ', 'பாலில் குழவி அலறவும்', 'நீரில் ... இனைகூஉ'. So the two do not judge one situation incompatibly. The poem shows the cost when the Kural's condition fails, which limits it rather than contradicting it, and 'two views of one siege' overstates this.

The shared word is real: the idyll's 'அந்தணர் பள்ளி' (474), and the Kural's 'அந்தணர் என்போர் அறவோர்'. But the idyll already puts 'அறநெறி பிழையா அன்புடை நெஞ்சின் பெரியோர்' (472) into its account, in the middle of the list and not last. So the claim that the couplet moves the definition 'to the one trait the idyll mentions last' misdescribes the idyll, and 'deliberate redefinition' of this poem is unsupported.

Both refuse his chest: the Kural's 'நண்ணேன் பரத்தநின் மார்பு' because women share him by sight, and Natrinai 174.10-11 'மல்லல் மார்பு மடுத்தனன் புல்லு மற்று எவனோ அன்பு இலங்கடையே'. But the Natrinai's grievance also includes a rival ('வீழ்ந்த கொண்டி', 9). It joins the two grievances rather than separating them, so the teaches sentence's division does not hold, and line 9 is of uncertain sense.
links.text_issue: natrinai 174.9 'வீழாக் கொள்கை வீழ்ந்த கொண்டி' is compressed and uncertain

links.reason: Both poems hold the same two images. The first is tusks bartered for toddy: 'யானை வெண்கோடு கொண்டு கள்கொடி நுடங்கும் ஆவணம் புக்(கு) ... நொடைமை' (68.9-11) against 'அண்ணல் யானை வெண்கோடு கொண்டு, நறவுநொடை' (61.9-10). The second is days scored on a wall: 'நெடும்சுவர் நாள்பல எழுதி' (68.17) against 'நாள்இழை நெடுஞ்சுவர்' (61.4). The Akananuru places the barter in Pulli's land and the wall at home, while Kapilar sets both in one king's campaign, so the pair shows a shared stock being redistributed.

Paripadal 2.16-17 names an age for the boar ('கேழல் திகழ்வரக் கோலமொடு பெயரிய ஊழி'). Paripadal 3.21-24 narrates the deed at an age's end ('தொகூஉம் ஊழி ஆழிக்கண், இரு நிலம், உரு கெழு கேழலாய் மருப்பின் உழுதோய்'). Together they show the boar as both a time-name and a told rescue, which neither hymn shows alone. Paripadal 2's opening is damaged, but lines 16-17 are intact.
links.text_issue: paripadal 2.1-2 has a lacuna and a strong variant; lines 7-8 repaired

links.reason: Both make pallor return the instant touch stops: the Kural's 'புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில் அள்ளிக்கொள் வற்றே பசப்பு' and Kuruntokai 399's 'பாசி யற்றே பசலை ... தொடுவுழித் தொடுவுழி நீங்கி விடுவுழி விடுவுழிப் பரத்த லானே'. The well-moss gives the couplet's instant onset a seen mechanism, including its repetition. 'Not exaggeration' is a little strong, but the development is real.

Ainkurunuru 324 has the traveller sure of the dream ('சிறிதுகண் படுப்பினும் காண்குவென் மன்ற'). Akananuru 39 has the same road-dream end in 'வறுங்கை காட்டிய வாய்அல் கனவின் ஏற்று ஏக்கற்ற உலமரல்' (23-24), which the returned man then offers as proof against 'உள்ளியும் அறிதிரோ, எம்?'. The second limits the first's comfort and puts it to use in the oodal, as the teaches sentence says.

poems.note: The crane that has fed in the backwater and sleeps through the roar of breaking waves maps to the man who has had his pleasure and rests untroubled while she pales.
The bird leaving the old tree it lived in by day 'புலம்ப' maps to the man, the abandoned tree to her loneliness, and the jackfruit slope he makes for to his errand.
Line 2 is obscure, so no secure second correspondence between the crowded flowers and the man's women can be named.
Lines 1-2 are obscure; the withered kodal marks the season's passing and carries mood only.

iraicchi.act: birds come to roost on the drooping njaazhal branch of his shore
iraicchi.sense: on his shore even the birds settle for the night, while he leaves her unable to sleep; he ought to give her the same shelter

poems.note: The cowherds who bring the cattle home do what the absent man should do, but they are people, not a native thing.
The sea and sand are openly likened to Mal and his brother; no love situation is stated for any mapping to point to.
The sweet comb that has fallen and is trampled under a calf's hoof maps to the girl's love given in secret and spoiled by his careless delay; the friend's demand for marriage states the situation.
The vehicle is a human scene: the poor woman's daughter left unswung by graceless men. Only the single match of neglect to the heroine is secure.

The river that runs muddy in the cold and gem-clear in summer maps to his changing favour, and its adorning his town is set against pallor adorning her eyes; the parallel அணிந்தன்று/அணிந்தன is juxtaposition, not a comparison marker.

iraicchi.act: the waves bring coral, pearl and crystal and heap them in the courtyard
iraicchi.sense: the sea already brings riches to her door, so he should come with gifts to marry her

poems.note: The female monkey and her untaught mate take the first millet the girl guards and eat it openly like ascetics, which maps to the lovers' secret taking now to be enjoyed openly; the colophon (வரைவு மலிந்த) states the coming marriage.
Line 2 is corrupt, so the opening images cannot be read.
Without the cloud's lines the 'கருவணி காலம்' he fixed loses its content: the cloud is the season sign itself.
The new hill water is prescribed literally as medicine (மருந்தும் ஆகும்), so the irony is stated rather than hidden.

ullurai.anchor: துறைவன் சொல்லிய சொல்என் இறையோர் எல்வளை கொண்டுநின் றதுவே

poems.note: The crow maps to the man and the small fish trapped in the cut-off backwater to the helpless girl he takes his fill of. Since the scene has two mapped parts, it is ullurai rather than iraicchi.
The flowers scattered like pearls off a broken string over every ford map to the talk spreading through the whole town once the secret is out.
Lines 1-3 describe Iruppai, the vehicle of an open simile for her beauty.

iraicchi.act: the birds go back to their roost at evening
iraicchi.sense: everything pairs and goes home at nightfall, so his parting from the guarded girl is pressing: he should marry her

poems.note: The birds stand beside the human couples (புணர்ந்தோர்) as causes of his sighing; they suggest rather than compare.
Line 2 (நிகரில் மடமான் எரியும்) is unclear, and no figure can be read from it.
